sections.h2: What is the principal residence exemption in Michigan?
sections.html:
It is a break on the school operating part of your property tax bill. Michigan's Treasury describes it as exempting an owner's principal residence from the local school operating millage, up to 18 mills (Treasury PRE page). The statute behind it is MCL 211.7cc.

People often call it the homestead exemption, but Michigan keeps the two ideas apart. The Homestead Property Tax Credit is a separate credit claimed on an income tax return. The exemption discussed here is claimed with the local assessor and shows up on the tax roll.

A principal residence is the one place where an owner has a true, fixed, and permanent home to which the owner intends to return whenever absent. It also reaches the owner's unoccupied residential or timber-cutover land that adjoins the dwelling and is owned and occupied by the owner (MCL 211.7dd(c)).

sections.h2: Who counts as an owner for the exemption?
sections.html:
Only an individual who holds a documented ownership interest. Treasury's ownership guidance says verbal agreements do not create an interest, and the person claiming carries the burden of proof. The groups it lists as eligible are below.

  • A person who owns the property, including a partial owner.
  • A land contract purchaser under a written contract that the seller signed.
  • A holder of a life estate, who is treated as a partial owner.
  • A beneficiary who receives ownership rights under a will, a trust, or intestate succession.
  • A grantor who placed the home in a revocable trust or a qualified personal residence trust.
  • A cooperative housing corporation or a registered life care facility.

An LLC, a corporation, a shareholder of a corporation, and a sole member of an LLC do not qualify. A trust is not itself an owner, though its grantor or beneficiaries may be. In a married couple that files a joint Michigan return, only one exemption is allowed (MCL 211.7cc(3)).

sections.h2: When and where do I file the affidavit?
sections.html:
File Form 2368, the Principal Residence Exemption Affidavit, with the assessor for the city or township where the home sits. The statute sets June 1 for the summer levy and November 1 for the winter levy (MCL 211.7cc(2)). A valid affidavit filed by June 1 reduces that year's bill starting with the summer levy. One filed from June 2 through November 1 reduces it starting with the winter levy.

The affidavit states that you own and occupy the property on the signing date and have not claimed a substantially similar break in another state. Claiming both brings a $500 penalty. Treasury also warns that a false claim can bring perjury charges, with penalties that include up to a year in jail and fines of $1,000 to $5,000 (MCL 211.120).

Closing agents and local assessors hand out the forms, and Treasury also posts them. The statute adds that a closing statement preparer who skips the forms is not legally liable for it, so the seller and buyer should ask for them.

sections.h2: What if I missed a deadline?
sections.html:
You can still file. Treasury says the owner may file Form 2368 with the local assessor at any time during the year, and the assessor may grant the exemption back through the current year and the three years before it, provided the owner met the requirements on June 1 or November 1 of each year claimed. If the owner has died, the estate can file for the same period.

Since July 11, 2022, the July and December Boards of Review no longer have authority to grant late claims. Only the assessor does, so go to the assessor's office rather than waiting for a board hearing.

sections.h2: How does the exemption work for two parcels, a duplex, or a split lot?
sections.html:
Each parcel needs its own affidavit. Treasury's example is an owner whose home sits on one parcel and whose contiguous residential land is a second parcel: both need Form 2368. When a parcel is split or combined, the new parcel numbers mean a fresh affidavit.

If the home is one unit of a multiple-unit dwelling, or a dwelling within a mixed-use building, the owner claims only the share of taxable value used as the principal residence, in the manner Treasury prescribes (MCL 211.7cc(16)). A landlord who lives in one side of a duplex therefore claims that side only. Ask the local assessor how the portion is measured before you file.

sections.h2: What must a seller do with the exemption?
sections.html:
The exemption lasts until December 31 of the year the property is transferred, or until it stops being a principal residence (MCL 211.7cc(4)). Within 90 days after you stop using the home as your principal residence you must file Form 2602 with the local tax collecting unit. Treasury lists several cases where rescission is still required: the owner dies, a spouse leaves after a divorce, or the owner moves out during a foreclosure redemption period.

There is one holding option if you moved and the house is for sale. An owner who claims the exemption on a new current residence can keep it on the old home for up to 3 tax years by filing a conditional rescission form, as long as the old home is unoccupied, listed for sale, not leased, and not used for business. Lease it and the local unit denies the conditional rescission back to the prior December 31.

An owner who moved into a nursing home or assisted living facility may keep the exemption if the home stays owned, no new principal residence is set up, the home is maintained, and it is not leased or used for business.

sections.h2: How are denials, audits, and back taxes handled?
sections.html:
An assessor who believes the home is not the owner's principal residence can deny a new or existing claim in writing, for the current year and up to the three years before. The owner has 35 days from the notice date to appeal to the residential and small claims division of the Michigan tax tribunal, and does not have to pay the disputed tax to appeal. Counties can elect to audit claims, and Treasury audits annually in counties that do not.

Back taxes carry interest at 1.25% per month or fraction of a month from the date they were last payable without penalty. If the home was sold to a bona fide purchaser before the extra bill went out, the tax, interest, and penalties are not a lien on the property and are not billed to that buyer. Treasury assesses the former owner instead. That protection is one reason a seller should rescind promptly.

A land contract buyer has one more filing: Treasury says the buyer must file a Property Transfer Affidavit, Form 2766, with the local assessor within 45 days of the transfer.

faqs.q: Does Michigan's exemption cover the whole property tax bill?
faqs.a: No. It removes the local school operating millage, up to 18 mills, from the bill. Millages other than local school operating still apply, so a bill drops but does not vanish.

faqs.q: Can I claim it on a cottage with a higher taxable value than my house?
faqs.a: No. Treasury says the exemption can be claimed only on the property that is the owner's true, fixed, and permanent home, and not on the basis of potential tax savings.

faqs.q: Do I have to file a new affidavit every year?
faqs.a: No. A valid claim stays on the property while the owner keeps meeting the requirements. A new affidavit is needed when a parcel is split or combined, because that creates new parcel numbers.

faqs.q: Who files the rescission when an owner dies?
faqs.a: The estate's personal representative or trustee files Form 2602 with the assessor within 90 days of death, because the deceased owner can no longer occupy the home or intend to return.

faqs.q: What if my trust owns the house?
faqs.a: The grantor or beneficiary who lives there signs Form 2368 in their own name, with the trust role noted. If the grantor cannot sign, the trustee may sign on the grantor's behalf, according to Treasury's claim guidance.
